item.title: Drake’s “Janice STFU” Accuser Withdraws Copyright Lawsuit
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Drake's "Janice STFU" copyright lawsuit was withdrawn by songwriter GoodbyeCalev after the rapper's team denied his claims.
item.content:encoded:
Drake saw the copyright lawsuit over “Janice STFU” withdrawn less than two weeks after a songwriter accused him of copying its chorus.

Rolling Stone reported that Aviel Calev Hirschfield voluntarily dismissed the lawsuit barely 10 days after filing it. The publication cited a recent court filing.

The Portland producer, known professionally as GoodbyeCalev, had sued Drake on October 16 in California federal court. The complaint also named OVO Sound LLC, UMG Recordings Inc. and Universal Music Publishing Inc.

Drake’s team had denied the claims and called the lawsuit “manufactured and baseless.” His representatives maintained that he wrote the song himself.

GoodbyeCalev’s complaint described a chorus he said he developed with Drake in mind over music from production duo FnZ. He alleged that he completed his demo around January 25, 2026, sent it to producers who worked with Drake and heard nothing back.

“Janice STFU’s chorus is literally identical to the Copyrighted Work in lyrics, melody, and cadence,” the complaint alleged.

The dispute involved more than what listeners heard. GoodbyeCalev alleged that his manager gave Drake’s representatives separate recording files and their metadata to support his account. He also alleged that Drake’s lawyers demanded he stop publicly claiming authorship.

A recording presented as his demo later circulated on X. A legal representative for GoodbyeCalev told Pitchfork that the leaked audio matched the recording submitted as evidence in the case. The producer’s claim rested on his account of when that recording was made.

The song’s musical roots were already public. “Janice STFU,” from Iceman, interpolated Lykke Li’s 2011 song “I Follow Rivers”. Drake had used Li’s music years earlier too, sampling “Little Bit” on his 2009 mixtape So Far Gone.

GoodbyeCalev and Drake also shared writing credits on Beyoncé’s “Heated,” from Renaissance. In a 2023 Willamette Week interview, GoodbyeCalev described how his manager circulated a track that Beyoncé picked up. He said the money from “Heated” helped him buy gear for his Southwest Portland studio after years working as a rapper, producer and engineer.

His now-withdrawn complaint sought damages and profits tied to the alleged infringement, along with a jury trial. It did not put a dollar figure on his claimed losses.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Lil Durk Offers Up Music Income To Get Out Of Jail, Lul Pab’s Mom Doesn’t Object
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: Lil Durk offered future music earnings as bond security after his acquittal, with Sony and major artists backing his release bid.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Durk put his future music income on the line in a new bond push, offering earnings he could lose if he fled.

His lawyers filed the proposal asking Judge Michael W. Fitzgerald to reconsider keeping the Chicago rapper behind bars after his recent acquittal.

The filing offered future royalties, publishing income, money tied to his name and image, touring earnings and cash and property from supporters.

“In support of his release, we offer a bond package so robust that should Mr. Banks violate his release conditions, both he and his family would be left destitute indefinitely,” his lawyers wrote.

Drew Findling, Marissa Goldberg, Brian Steel and Christy O’Connor submitted the brief, which said that while prosecutors opposed release, the slain man’s family did not.

In an attached September 28 letter, Andrea Robinson, mother of Saviay’a “Lul Pab” Robinson, left that decision to the judge considering the rapper’s request.

“On behalf of the family of Saviay’a Robinson, we do not object to Durk Banks being granted a bond if it is deemed appropriate by the Honorable Court,” she wrote.

The federal case grew out of an August 19, 2022 shooting near Los Angeles’ Beverly Center that killed Pab. Prosecutors alleged the intended target was his cousin, rapper Quando Rondo, whose legal name is Tyquian Bowman.

They accused Durk of financing a murder-for-hire plot that sent gunmen after Quando Rondo in Los Angeles. The government claimed the attack was retaliation for the November 2020 killing of King Von during a confrontation involving an associate of Quando Rondo.

Authorities took Durk into custody in October 2024, and he denied the accusations. On September 11, 2026, a jury acquitted him on five murder-for-hire and stalking counts heard in the first trial.

The verdict left him in custody because he also faces separate murder-in-aid-of-racketeering and firearms charges that remained pending, with another trial still ahead. He pleaded not guilty and now wants to be released.

“Following eleven days of evidence and argument and three days of deliberation, the jury unanimously found that Mr. Banks did not beyond a reasonable doubt participate in the conspiracy to stalk Mr. Bowman that ended in Mr. Robinson’s death,” the lawyers wrote.

They also argued that the verdict weakened the court’s earlier concerns about flight and possible interference with witnesses who testified against him.

“The jury’s full acquittal of Mr. Banks sends a clear message about his chances of success at a second trial, and diminishes the likelihood that he would violate his bond conditions should he be released,” the defense wrote.

His lawyers cited an earlier ruling to explain why the new offer went beyond the cash and property already proposed as security.

“[Lil Durk] would still have his intellectual property with which to earn a handsome living abroad. Any set of conditions would need to impoverish [Lil Durk] and lead to the forfeiture of all interest in his intellectual property,” Judge Fitzgerald wrote in the earlier order.

So, the new offer covers digital radio royalties plus publishing rights from Durk’s albums Almost Healed and Deep Thoughts, according to his lawyers.

It also included merchandise, branding and other income tied to his name, image and likeness. Touring completed the four streams, though lawyers acknowledged he could not tour while on the run.

“Mr. Banks offers to encumber each of these future income streams,” his lawyers wrote. “Of course, this encumbrance on his intellectual property is in addition to the other significant collateral: the home that Mr. Banks’ mother lives in, and a significant sum of cash and property proffered by friends who have placed their trust in Mr. Banks.”

Sony Music Entertainment backed part of the proposal in a September 14 letter signed by executive Stephanie Yu and included with the court papers.

“This letter will serve as confirmation that Sony Music Entertainment is prepared to guarantee an appearance bond for Mr. Banks up to an amount of $1,000,000,” Yu wrote.

“Separately, we have also agreed that Mr. Banks is allowed to forfeit his future earnings toward the bond in an amount to be determined by this Honorable Court.”

Letters from JAY-Z, J. Cole, Michael Rubin and former Cook County State’s Attorney Kim Foxx also supported the request or described Durk’s character and community work.

The defense said therapy, sobriety and his Muslim faith had changed his life before his arrest. The filing said he completed a 30-day inpatient drug treatment program with encouragement from his wife, India.

JAY-Z’s letter described Durk helping young artists from his community secure recording contracts, giving them work in music and a route beyond limited neighborhood opportunities.

Cole explained that Durk insisted on the hopeful message behind their collaboration “All My Life,” even after Cole asked him for a different song.

“He wanted to push a message of change and of peace and of growth and maturity, and he thought that if I got on this song with him it would have the greatest impact,” J. Cole wrote.

item.title: Romeo Miller Joins Hulu’s “The Mob”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Romeo Miller joined Hulu's "The Mob," a celebrity competition with Parker Posey and up to $250,000 in cash prizes at stake.
item.content:encoded:
Romeo Miller joined Hulu’s “The Mob,” putting the rapper in a villa with 11 other celebrities with up to $250,000 in cash prizes at stake.

The reality competition premiered Monday, October 26. Parker Posey hosts and also serves as an executive producer.

According to Hulu, the group picks a don who controls who gets paid, stays or leaves. The others can overthrow that leader. Each episode brings jobs drawn from mob movies, with the cast competing in an Italian villa.

Some of Miller’s castmates have played their own parts in crime families on screen.

Aida Turturro played Tony Soprano’s sister Janice on “The Sopranos.” Debi Mazar’s credits include “Goodfellas,” “Entourage,” and “Younger.” Their acting careers put them alongside reality stars from dating shows and Bravo.

Joe Gorga, of “The Real Housewives of New Jersey,” is Melissa Gorga’s husband and Teresa Giudice’s brother.

Harry Jowsey has appeared on “Too Hot to Handle,” “Dancing With the Stars,” and “Let’s Marry Harry.” Maria Georgas entered “The Bachelor” during Season 28, when Joey Graziadei was the lead, before joining this cast. Willam Belli competed on Season 4 of “RuPaul’s Drag Race” and also works as an actor and recording artist.

Miller already had years of TV work behind him before this cast came together. As Lil Romeo, he built a rap career and had his own Nickelodeon series, “Romeo!,” which ran from 2003 to 2006.

The son of Master P later appeared on “Growing Up Hip Hop”, alongside Angela Simmons, Rev. Run’s daughter, and Boogie Dash, Damon Dash’s son. By July 2017, Miller was among the returning cast members as that series entered its third season.

The show followed the children of music stars as they told their own stories.

U.S. viewers can watch on Hulu, including through Hulu on Disney+ with a bundle subscription. Outside the United States, the series is available on Disney+.

item.title: Megan Thee Stallion Explains How Silence Over Her Contract Led To Regret & Legal War
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Megan Thee Stallion revisited her early contract fears as her music business moved toward ownership and creative control.
item.content:encoded:
Megan Thee Stallion said she once feared questioning her record deal. She spoke at Overcoming Impossible Live at 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge in New York City.

Entrepreneur and Robert Irvine organized the event for business owners. The program paired small-group work with afternoon talks from Megan, Gary Vaynerchuk and Irvine.

“I was a little bit nervous about asking questions,” she told Entrepreneur.

What followed were years of fights over her music.

As AllHipHop previously reported, Megan signed with Carl Crawford’s 1501 Certified Entertainment in 2018 and sued the label in 2020. In October 2023, the two sides settled and parted ways. They kept the terms private.

During that dispute, Megan accused 1501 of blocking releases and keeping her under contract after she had fulfilled its terms. She also sought outside oversight of the label’s finances to ensure it could pay a potential judgment. Crawford disputed that request and accused her of using it to harass the label.

“I started realizing I’m not making as much money as I should be making because I kind of just gave my life away to somebody else,” Megan Thee Stallion said. “I had to take a step back and think, Okay, let me see what’s going on with my contracts. Let me figure out how I can be my own boss.”

Her next deals put ownership at the center. In February 2024, Warner Music Group announced an agreement that left Megan with her masters and publishing.

Releases would come through her own Hot Girl Productions, with Warner providing distribution and help with radio and marketing. She also kept creative control. She could bring artists signed to her imprint into Warner’s network if she chose.

She had already started releasing music through her own company before the Warner deal.

“Cobra” arrived in November 2023. In its announcement, Warner counted “HISS” as the second solo song she released through her company.

A more recent deal continued that approach.

On August 14, 2026, Megan announced a distribution partnership with Interscope Records. The announcement said Hot Girl Productions would remain home for her releases, and she would keep her masters and publishing while receiving global distribution and strategic support.

“I’ve always wanted to create music on my terms while building a legacy that extends beyond the industry,” Megan said in that announcement.

item.title: Hit-Boy Turns Roblox Players Into Remix Rivals In “Beat Battle”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Hit-Boy brought a monthlong remix season to Roblox's Beat Battle, where players can use his vocals and earn game rewards.
item.content:encoded:
Hit-Boy is bringing his music to Roblox’s Beat Battle, letting fans build beats with his vocals and go head-to-head with other players.

The month-long season lets players pull apart 10 tracks from his album HITStory 2: Success is a Dirty Word. The game’s first artist collaboration offers drums, bass, synths and vocals for remixing.

The competition puts players on the clock. Battles use changing vocal clips that run 25 seconds.

Players present their mixes, vote and earn Season Tickets, which unlock Hit-Boy beat packs, clothes and DJ decks. Some packs can be earned through play, while players can also buy music and merchandise in the game, the report said.

Those tools have a limit: Roblox won’t let players export raw audio or separate vocal stems.

The official Beat Battle page lists the Hit-Boy season as live. Overtune, the game’s developer, describes a setup where players can remix loops or make their own music with a piano roll.

Friends can battle onstage and vote on performances. Players can also unlock stages and effects, grow their music collections and share tracks with friends. The game puts making music, performing it and judging other players’ work in the same space.

HarbourView Equity Partners put the collaboration together with Roblox, Overtune and the producer’s team.

That adds a gaming project to a business relationship announced in November 2025.

HarbourView’s announcement said the firm would work with Hit-Boy on future titles he wrote. Its announcement described the agreement as exclusive and said the relationship had begun that summer.

The firm invests in music and other entertainment businesses.

The partnership followed his exit from an 18-year publishing deal with Universal Music Publishing Group.

AllHipHop previously reported that he signed the agreement at 19 and thanked JAY-Z and Roc Nation CEO Desiree Perez for helping him get out. He marked that break with the song “What’s The Deal?”

When HarbourView announced their partnership, Hit-Boy laid out what he wanted from his next business moves.

“This next chapter of my career is about ownership, being innovative and my creative freedom,” he said.

item.title: NE-YO Takes World Series Stage For Game 4 National Anthem
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: NE-YO will sing the national anthem at World Series Game 4 in St. Petersburg, with Hailey Riggs providing ASL interpretation.
item.content:encoded:
NE-YO will sing the national anthem before World Series Game 4 on Tuesday, October 27, bringing the R&B star to Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Hailey Riggs will provide American Sign Language interpretation during the performance, according to WFLA.

Major League Baseball confirmed his appearance, with FOX’s coverage set to begin at 7 p.m. ET.

The booking comes in a year that marks two decades since his debut album, In My Own Words. The 2006 release topped the Billboard 200. Since then, the three-time Grammy winner has built a career both at the microphone and behind other artists’ songs.

His catalog includes “So Sick,” “Sexy Love,” “Closer,” and “Miss Independent.” Beyond his own records, he has written Beyoncé’s “Irreplaceable” and Rihanna’s “Unfaithful,” “Russian Roulette,” and “Take a Bow.” He also earned his first diamond-certified song through “Give Me Everything,” his collaboration with Pitbull and Afrojack.

This summer, he took his music toward country with Highway 79. Released July 10, the 11-song album was recorded in Nashville and included “Thinking What I’m Thinking,” “Up Out & Gone” and “Ms. Tundra.” Apple Music’s album notes describe a project that brought country influences into his R&B sound.

That expansion followed a different kind of stage assignment. He made his Broadway debut as Davis in Alicia Keys’ “Hell’s Kitchen,” beginning December 4, 2025. The musical used Keys’ songs to tell the story of a 17-year-old girl named Ali. He had previously played the Tin Man in NBC’s “The Wiz Live!”

The move into musical theater put him in a role built around another artist’s catalog. His work had already crossed into film and television, including “Stomp The Yard” and “World Of Dance.”

Long before those later bookings, he spoke to AllHipHop about learning to love performing. In the 2006 interview, he said songwriting had initially felt more comfortable.

Watching recordings of his earliest shows also made him see how much he had loosened up.

Even then, he said his tastes went well beyond Hip-Hop and R&B. He named country, folk, rock and heavy metal among the styles he enjoyed.

“I’ve always loved to sing, and I’ve developed such a craving for a stage,” he said.

item.title: Krayzie Bone’s Youth Foundation To Benefit From Ohio Hip Hop Awards Reunion
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Krayzie Bone's Spread the Love Foundation will share proceeds from the Ohio Hip Hop Awards' November 1 reunion dinner.
item.content:encoded:
Krayzie Bone‘s push to help young people find work in music will get support from a Cleveland reunion this weekend. The Ohio Hip Hop Awards will mark its 20th anniversary with a dinner that will raise money for his Spread the Love Foundation and DJ Johnny O’s Nerve DJ Institute.

The event is set for Sunday, November 1, at Music Box Supper Club, 1148 Main Avenue in Cleveland. Doors and the red carpet open at 4 p.m., and the main program starts at 6 P.M.

Organizers say a portion of the proceeds will go to each nonprofit. Spread the Love focuses on youth career training and arts education. The Nerve DJ Institute helps aspiring DJs and other young music professionals build skills through training and mentorship.

For Krayzie, that work has already reached young people in detention. As AllHipHop previously reported, his foundation brought its Interest 2 Income program to the Cuyahoga County Juvenile Detention Center, teaching participants about music careers and creative work.

The foundation’s program goes beyond trying to make students the next star onstage. Its youth track serves ages 13 to 17 and introduces the business and creative jobs that keep music moving.

The foundation lists sound engineering, audio production and songwriting among the skills taught through its work at the county’s juvenile justice center.

That training has led to finished music. The county reported that eight detention center residents graduated from the program’s introductory course on October 18, 2024. They performed songs they had written and recorded, along with a group song, while family members watched.

The course covered money skills, entrepreneurship and personal growth.

Sunday’s dinner will also look back at Ohio’s music scene. The board announced that the Ohio Hip Hop Awards began in 2006 and ran through 2017. Organizers plan to show previously unseen clips, share backstage stories and revisit memories from the OHHA Showcase Tour.

Shugabooga will host the event, with music from DJ Iceburg Pimpin’.

Reserved tickets cost $25, $50 and $100, according to the venue’s official event listing. Guests are asked to wear chic cocktail attire.

item.title: GloRilla Renews Steelers Anthem Pledge
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: GloRilla renewed her plan for a Pittsburgh Steelers anthem as she prepared for a November concert and another football visit.
item.content:encoded:
GloRilla still wants to give the Pittsburgh Steelers a song of their own, and she renewed that pledge ahead of her upcoming Pittsburgh concert.

The Memphis rapper told Pittsburgh City Paper she planned to follow through on an anthem for her favorite NFL team.

“I keep saying I’m going to do it, but I am,” she said. “I need to shout out the Steelers.”

Her loyalty dates to age 3. She said her father told her that her grandmother, who died before GloRilla was born, also supported the team.

The song idea has been around for a while. In April 2024, SteelerNation reported that she discussed making a Steelers record on “The Pivot.” She pointed to Wiz Khalifa’s “Black And Yellow” as the model and stressed that she wanted to find the right song.

That comparison comes with some real Pittsburgh history.

Wiz Khalifa performed “Black And Yellow” before the Steelers’ January 2011 AFC Championship game against the New York Jets, where he joined actor Billy Gardell for the Terrible Towel Twirl before kickoff.

As for GloRilla, she is working with the NFL’s “NFL City Life,” which paired the Memphis rapper with receiver George Pickens in Pittsburgh to document her support for the team.

Her next trip includes a concert. Live Nation lists her at Citizens Live at The Wylie on Monday, November 2 at 8 P.M., her first Pittsburgh headlining show. She told City Paper she planned to attend the Steelers’ home game the day before her show.

Outside of football, she has also been building GloVerse, her beauty-tech venture. The platform connects clients with beauty professionals, a business she developed after struggling to find glam services while traveling.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: RBX Loses Spotify Bot Lawsuit Again After Judge Rejects Latest Attempt
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: RBX lost his Spotify bot lawsuit after a judge dismissed his revised claims and ruled that another rewrite would be futile.
item.content:encoded:
RBX lost his Spotify bot lawsuit after a federal judge rejected his revised claims and wouldn’t let him refile.

U.S. District Judge Josephine L. Staton dismissed the West Coast rapper’s negligence and California Unfair Competition Law claims with prejudice in an order AllHipHop reviewed.

That closed the door to another amended complaint in this case.

The dispute centered on who loses money when fake plays inflate an artist’s share of Spotify streams. RBX, whose legal name is Eric Dwayne Collins, claimed bots boosted major acts, including Drake, while shrinking the royalty shares of other music rights holders. Drake was not a defendant.

RBX filed suit on November 2, 2025. Judge Staton dismissed his first complaint on June 22 but let him try again.

As AllHipHop previously reported, his revised suit accused Spotify of using stricter fraud controls against smaller artists while letting bigger names escape the same scrutiny.

That new argument did not save the case. The order said RBX failed to identify a specific fraud-control rule that Spotify enforced against some artists but ignored for others. Instead, he pointed to minimum stream and listener requirements that could hurt smaller acts more than stars.

The negligence claim failed because the court found no special duty requiring Spotify to protect RBX from third-party bots. Spotify’s greater power in the music business did not turn their commercial ties into that kind of protective relationship.

On Spotify’s role, Judge Staton wrote: “That streaming activity on Spotify’s platform may impact [RBX’s] career and status does not transform Spotify’s role into one of a protector.”

The court also rejected an argument that Spotify took on that duty through its anti-fraud efforts. That legal theory required physical harm, which RBX had not claimed.

Spotify’s published anti-fraud policy said detected fake plays did not earn royalties or count toward public stream totals. The court also said the presence of bots did not show that Spotify had failed to carry out its stated daily cleanups.

Judge Staton also found that RBX had claimed losses as a music rights holder without showing harm to Spotify’s consumers or competitors, another problem for his unfair-business claim.

As for another rewrite, Judge Staton wrote: “The Court finds that further leave to amend would be futile.”

Spotify’s separate request to strike the class allegations was denied as moot. The court ordered the company to submit a proposed judgment within five days of the order.

item.title: Jakarta Government Reveals Massive Economic Impact Of Ye’s Concert
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Ye's Jakarta concert brought an estimated $25 million in economic activity to the city, Governor Pramono Anung said.
item.content:encoded:
Ye‘s Jakarta concert generated an estimated $25 million in economic activity, according to Governor Pramono Anung.

The governor shared that estimate Monday, October 26, following the rapper’s Saturday performance at Gelora B### Karno Main Stadium.

The official report also put ticket sales at about $18 million, while Pramono said hotels, shops, transport and tourism benefited.

That account offered no detailed breakdown of how officials arrived at the broader estimate of the concert’s economic impact.

Before the show, promoter Raw Vision Collective said 20,500 people outside Indonesia had bought tickets, according to Indonesia Expat.

Karen Tjahja, who led marketing and communications for the promoter, gave that sales update at an October 22 press conference. Among buyers abroad, Australia ranked first, with Singapore and Malaysia following it in the promoter’s count of international ticket sales.

Those figures captured purchases ahead of the concert, leaving them separate from a final tally of fans inside the stadium.

Tjahja said other events that week had made flights harder to find, prompting the promoter to arrange extra charter services.

Tjahja said the overseas sales could mark a new high for international visitors at an Indonesian solo concert.

The concert had offered fans a hotel option from the start, with packages advertised when tickets went on sale in July.

AllHipHop’s earlier coverage described the October 24 booking as the only Southeast Asian date on Ye’s 2026 tour schedule.

Organizers then expected as many as 77,000 people, a pre-show projection that didn’t indicate how many ultimately attended Saturday.

The stop also returned him to a region where he had played Singapore Indoor Stadium in 2008 and SingFest in 2010.

The tour also featured The Globe Stage, a 360-degree production designed to put fans around the performance and inside the experience.

MRT Jakarta’s Mega Tarigan, its director of operations and maintenance, announced the transit changes Friday, October 23.

MRT Jakarta also announced longer train hours for fans and the public, extending service until 1:30 a.m. Sunday, October 25.
